items.title: Giulio Ciccone Questions European Championships Photo Finish Against Remco Evenepoel
items.author: ahood
items.content: ‘I’ve watched the available footage hundreds of times’: The Italian wants to see the decisive image after missing European gold by 0.0028 seconds.
items.lbText:
Ciccone reacts after losing the European Championships in a photo finish. (Photo: Getty Images)

Giulio Ciccone wants to see the image that decided the European road title for himself, because he still has doubts about Sunday’s razor-thin defeat .

The Italian said he still cannot come to terms with the photo finish verdict and footage of his dramatic loss against Remco Evenepoel .

“The title was awarded by a margin of 0.0028 seconds, or 2.8 thousandths of a second,” Ciccone wrote on Instagram.

“I’ve watched the available footage hundreds of times and, in the shots where the finish line is visible, I keep seeing something that I cannot reconcile with that verdict.”

Evenepoel snagged gold Sunday with a spectacular bike throw in Slovenia to edge out the Italian in a two-up sprint so tight that it took a photo finish to call the winner.

On Monday, Ciccone praised the Belgian’s performance and defended his racing tactics, but said he wanted to see the evidence for himself.

“Remco was the strongest rider yesterday,” he wrote. “I’m asking for something very simple: to see the photo finish at the actual finish line.”

Ciccone said commissaires and federation technical staff explained Monday morning how the photo finish works and the criteria used to interpret it.

But that’s not enough for the 31-year-old Lidl-Trek star to accept the outcome.

items.title: Formula 1 Superstar Valtteri Bottas Is Cycling From Malaysia to Singapore for His Next Grand Prix
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Some drivers would take a private jet for the long journey from Sepang to Singapore – but not Bottas, the F1 racer-turned gravel aficionado.
items.lbText:
Valtteri Bottas is decompressing from a disappointing DNF at Sunday’s Grand Prix in Malaysia by cycling some 350km to his next race.

It’s not the usual way Formula 1 drivers choose to recover from the mind-zapping fatigue and furnace-like conditions of a 300kph race in stormy Southeast Asia.

But it’s the way that F1’s elite gravel cycling convert has decided will work for him.

On Sunday night, Bottas completed “Leg 1” of a multi-day adventure ride toward this coming weekend’s Singapore Grand Prix.

The 37-year-old Cadillac driver had spun out on lap nine of a wet and wild race on the Sepang International Circuit on Sunday, which was being used as a substitute venue for the originally planned race in Bahrain.

Not long after stripping out of his overalls, Bottas clocked 56km in little more than two hours of night-time riding heading southeast toward Si Rusa.

The veteran car driver and Canyon bikes ambassador posted a video to Instagram showing him bumping his way across gravelly trails, followed by a #foodporn photo of a boutique dinner upon arrival in the popular tourist spot on the Malaysian coast.

With a base salary of around $5 million USD, Bottas hardly needs to “dirtbag” his journey, after all.

Bottas is famed for his off-the-racetrack exploits.

items.title: ‘My Shape Is Really Bad’: Tadej Pogačar Sorry/Not Sorry to Miss Euro Champs
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Speculation growing about when and where Pogačar could return to racing in 2027. His team and others comment.
items.lbText:
Tadej Pogačar and his partner Urska Žigart attend the elite men's European road race championships as spectators (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski/Getty Images) (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski)

There was much chatter recently that Tadej Pogačar might defy team orders and ride the European championships , both to defend his title and also because it was held in his home country of Slovenia.

His team denied it and said his recovery was too important, and so it proved: the 28 year old was at the race, but only as a guest.

Winning a major title on home soil is likely a once in a lifetime possibility for a Slovenian but, in this case at least, it’s one ambition he may have to let go of.

Ditto for his partner Urška Žigart, who is also sidelined after a jawbone fracture reoccurred again.

“For sure even yesterday when we were watching the women’s race, Urška was like, ‘damn, I should be there,” Pogačar told Eurosport after the finish of Sunday’s race.

“Especially she has been feeling super good so it is tough. When you have good shape it is tough to look at the race and know you could be part of it.”

Pogačar has been in dominant form this year, winning a record-equaling fifth Tour de France plus multiple other races. He looked to be en route for victory at the Vuelta a España but crashed heavily on stage 8 and withdrew.

items.title: Evenepoel Pips Ciccone in Desperate Sprint to Become European Champion
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Remco Evenepoel, crashes, recovers, attacks, does all the work and finally pips Ciccone in photo finish.
items.lbText:
Remco Evenepoel beats Giulio Ciccone to become European road race champion in Sencur, Slovenia. (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski/Getty Images) (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski)

Remco Evenepoel found redemption after a disappointing road race at the world championships, becoming European road race champ for the first time in his pro career after a dramatic finale.

The Belgian outsprinted Giulio Ciccone (Italy) at the line but had to wait for the result of a photo finish to confirm the win. Ciccone got a better line through the last corner and opened a lead of several bike lengths, but lost out by a tiny margin.

Evenepoel was fueled by pride and stubbornness, being determined to show well after his worlds disappointment and going into hulk mode after he went clear with Ciccone on the penultimate lap but crashed.

He took an uphill bend too fast and lost his front wheel, with his Belgian team keeping him within range and enabling him to jump up to Ciccone once again.

The Italian declined to work on the final lap, taking only one brief turn near the finish, and took the final corner better.

This gave him an important gap over Evenepoel but the Belgian wouldn’t be denied, chasing furiously all the way to the line and then lunging past. His throw to the line was better than that of Ciccone and this was just enough to give him the victory.

items.title: Pogačar’s Viral Booty Band Warm-Up Routine Might Just Be a Placebo
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Should cyclists warm up with mini bands? Why the placebo effect might outweigh any true muscle 'activation,' and how riders can make better use of glute bands.
items.lbText:
Tadej Pogačar made “booty bands” everybody’s favorite warm-up ritual when he was filmed twerking and squatting his way through a pre-race routine, bands around his knees.

But it turns out that these wildly popular pre-ride workouts might largely be a placebo .

Waddling, lunging, and squatting through a mini-band session before a ride doesn’t “activate your glutes” or prime you to push max power.

According to WorldTour experts, the power of glute bands might largely be in the mind.

“These mini band moves are beneficial, but it’s more from a pseudo-science perspective. Someone riders might feel like, ‘Oh, I’m doing something , I’m preparing myself to ride’ by doing them,” Jayco-AlUla physiotherapist Dan Guillemette told Velo .

“But in terms of actual performance, it’s really unlikely there’s any actual benefit.”

So how have mini-bands become one of sport’s most popular primers?

They’ve become no-brainers for WorldTour and triathlon pros, TikTok influencers, 4w/kg Velo writers [ ahem ], and everyone in between.

Here’s why mini band warm-ups might not be worth your time – unless you’re already doing them – and how to make better use of these wildly popular home workout tools.

Pogačar’s pre-race warm-up video was one of the viral cycling clips of 2025. The meme pages loved it.

items.title: Ezra Caudell Leaves the Hospital 31 Days After Philadelphia Crash
items.author: ahood
items.content: Modern Adventure rider Ezra Caudell will begin intensive rehabilitation as his recovery from the Philadelphia crash progresses, officials confirmed Tuesday.
items.lbText:
Ezra Caudell, shown here this spring, has left a hospital after a month following his crash. (Photo: Gautier Demouveaux/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Ezra Caudell has left the hospital and is transferring into intensive rehabilitation some 31 days after his traumatic crash at the Philadelphia Cycling Classic .

The Modern Adventure Pro Cycling rider was discharged late last week and will continue his recovery at Magee Rehabilitation Hospital in Philadelphia, officials confirmed.

Caudell, 20, was already walking the hospital halls before his discharge , according to the recovery update shared by his family and team.

“Just as encouraging has been his neurologic recovery. Ezra continues to show significant improvement from the injury to his brain, with progress in his strength, cognition, communication, and independence each day,” an update read.

“His recovery will take time, but his progress over the past month has been remarkable, and to see him now walking, interacting with those around him, and moving on to rehabilitation represents an enormous milestone.”

Caudell crashed on August 30 while racing the Philadelphia Cycling Classic.

The move into rehabilitation marks a major step for Caudell, though the team update on Tuesday emphasized that a long recovery still lies ahead.

The medical team expects his lung contusions and his fractures to continue healing without the need for further intervention, officials said.

items.title: Fractured Neck, Broken Collarbone, Relegation: Coppa Bernocchi Crash Takes Heavy Toll
items.author: ahood
items.content: Raccagni could face surgery, Aranburu’s season is over, and Van den Berg loses third after a chaotic, crash-marred final 600 meters at Coppa Bernocchi. And that's not counting a delivery van that drove onto the course.
items.lbText:
Ben Swift, inset, finished with cuts and gashes after a big crash at the end of Coppa Bernocchi. (Photo: Getty Images)

Andrea Raccagni fractured a neck vertebra and Alex Aranburu broke his collarbone and part of his pelvis in a brutal, high-speed crash Monday at the Coppa Bernocchi .

Marijn van den Berg (EF Education-EasyPost) lost his podium place after the race jury relegated him in a messy finale to the Italian classic.

The pileup tore through the bunch about 600 meters from the finish in Legnano as riders were fighting for position ahead of a reduced bunch sprint.

Netcompany-Ineos riders Ben Swift and Filippo Ganna were among those gong down in the crash, and one rider smashed heavily into an unpadded light post.

Swift — who is retiring this season — crossed the line with cuts and gashes, but is still hoping to race Paris-Tours later this month.

Raccagni suffered a fracture of his third cervical vertebra, Soudal Quick-Step confirmed after hospital examinations that included a CT scan. The Italian was scheduled for assessment by surgeons Tuesday.

“He will be assessed by surgeons tomorrow to determine the most appropriate course of treatment and recovery,” the team said in its Monday statement.

Aranburu sustained fractures to his right collarbone and iliac wing, a part of the pelvis, Cofidis announced.

The race jury relegated Van den Berg, who crossed the line third, to 33rd to last in the finishing group after a wild race in the mid-week classic.

items.title: The Kenda Velora Tire Review: Modern Endurance Road
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The new premium road offering from Kenda brings a lot more puncture protection and improved speed to its endurance platform.
items.lbText:
Kenda has launched the Velora Endurance, a new set of endurance road tires that offer a premium feel with a range of puncture-resistant long-haul options.

The Velora brings durability and low rolling resistance to the table, with Kenda claiming major improvements in puncture protection and watts saved over its previous models. The model also comes in three sizes: 28, 32, and 35 mm.

With Kenda’s re-entry into the premium endurance tire market—in addition to other tires like the Silca Protocol RCR —the 32-40 mm range for all-road tires is quickly filling out. Not too long ago, that range of tires was a quirky grey area between road and gravel, but now it serves as another area of the industry where there are scores of good options.

Read on to see how the Kenda Velora Endurance fits into the mix. Hint: it’s one of the better options available.

While the Velora Endurance brings new options to the endurance/all-road tire market, Kenda is taking a fairly traditional approach overall with this model. It’s built, first and foremost, for durability.

That durability is derived primarily from the puncture-resistant base layer of the tire casing. Instead of loading puncture-resistance features into the entire tread, the base layer runs just along the center of the tread. This keeps the tire weight low and the tire relatively thin, despite the 35 percent improvement in the center tread’s ability to withstand debris and detritus.

items.title: Silca Protocol RCR 29 Review: Go Bigger
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Silca built a 29mm tire with great ride feel, but that fails to stand out in any strong way. If you want to beat the competition, you have to look at a different size.
items.lbText:
Comfortable ride feel Excellent dry cornering grip High puncture resistance for a race tire Competitive weight-to-width ratio Aerodynamically optimized width Excellent choice in 38mm size

Silca recently launched a new series of tires. The lineup covers both road and gravel, and everything offered is focused on high volume and ride feel. Of course, they launched without much of a bang, and there definitely weren’t any major claims made… No, I am obviously kidding. This is Silca, and these tires launched to so much hype it hurt. The claim was that they were head and shoulders above the rest of the field.

Then Bicycle Rolling Resistance put the RCR 29 through its testing regime, and the results were… a bit lackluster. Big claims have now been made on the other side of the fence, but not that many people have actually ridden these tires. I’ve now got a few hundred miles on them, and I think there’s more to these tires than a drum test—but I don’t love everything. Let’s look at the good and the bad when it comes to the Silca RCR 29 road tires.

What I do on a bike—almost always a race bike—is ride it longer than anyone expects. I want a tire that soaks up rough pavement, but I’m not running 34mm tires because I also want aerodynamics in a straight line, and I’m not interested in increasing wheel width (meaning weight) to optimize for a wider tire. In other words, I want to have my cake and eat it too.

items.title: ‘Speak With Data’: UAE Boss Slams Skeptics Fueling Del Toro-McNulty Conspiracy Theories
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: McNulty and Del Toro's trade team manager defends Mexican amid talk of illegal collusion with USA at world championships: 'He was strongest, even if McNulty won.'
items.lbText:
Did Isaac del Toro help his UAE trade teammate Brandon McNulty win the road world title?

That’s the debate that’s doing the rounds after McNulty brought the U.S. its first rainbow jersey in 33 years at the UCI road world championships last weekend.

“Del Toro was obviously working for McNulty,” gnashed Tom Pidcock in the aftermath of a wild race in Montréal.

Michael Matthews insinuated similar as Team USA’s losing rivals picked apart what went wrong last Sunday.

The Tin Foil Hat Brigade has been picking over race replays and sparking conspiracy theories ever since.

Was there a nefarious trade team alliance in this race of nations?

Speaking to QuiBici Sport , McNulty and Del Toro’s manager at UAE Emirates-XRG dismissed the doubters.

If the Mexican Del Toro somehow colluded with Team USA after McNulty slipped away with his decisive attack, Joxean Fernández Matxin wants to see proof.

“To anyone who insinuates this, I urge you to speak with data and not with opinions,” Matxin told Qui Bici Sport . “How long was Del Toro on the front? And the others who are talking, how long were they on the front trying to close it down?

“If you bring me evidence with numbers showing that he pulled less than the others, then I can agree with you,” Matxin said. “But if they are just words, with all due respect, it remains an opinion we can all form.”

Matxin’s words of defense are hardly a surprise.

items.title: What’s Brandon McNulty’s Road Worlds Title Worth? Not Much, and a Lot
items.author: ahood
items.content: Analysis: Brandon McNulty earned €8,000 for his road world title. What could bonuses, contracts, and sponsors add to his payday?
items.lbText:
McNulty celebrates the world title in Montréal and it remains to be seen how much economic windfall it will deliver. (Photo: Filip Bezdek/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Brandon McNulty ended America’s 33-year drought for a men’s UCI road world title in Montréal, beat a field stacked with cycling’s biggest stars, and earned himself a rainbow jersey.

But the prize money alone won’t make him rich.

That’s the official paycheck for winning one of the sport’s most coveted races. Michael Matthews earned €4,000 for silver, Mathieu van der Poel collected €2,000 for bronze, and everyone else earned no official prize money.

Of course, McNulty was chasing a place in cycling history, not a down payment on a yacht, when he won America’s first elite men’s road title since Lance Armstrong in 1993 .

But what are those stripes really worth?

The prize money is the same for men and women in Montréal, but things get potentially more lucrative once agents, team bonuses, sponsorship deals, and long-term contracts enter the calculation.

First off, professional riders earn their paycheck from their respective trade teams, not from chasing the rainbow bands.

Racing the worlds with national teams is a unique, one-off event each season where money isn’t the primary motivation. It’s for the love of the game.

In fact, racing for the national team rarely earns the riders any extra dosh at all.
